This file describes the files of the project and how to regenerate the analysis. The aim and the main results are in `README.md`; the shell commands for
cleaning up and for running everything in order are in `cleanup.Rmd`.

# The files

| File | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `Supplementary_1_The_PUBS_data_and_preprocessing.Rmd` | Loads and preprocesses the US Census PUMS/ACS wage data: selects the employed full-time workers (1,061,763 people), makes the 500,000-row `Xtrain`, orders the categorical variables by mean log wage and makes the numeric `X_ordered_numeric`, and the code-to-description mappings. Runs as a script (`render`) from the raw data and has tests (`Supplementary_1_tests.txt`) |
| `Supplementary_2_First_Look_at_the_Data.Rmd` | Establishes the analysis sample. Documents the dependent-children problem with `children` and restricts the age to 26–53 (659,436 people), caps the Census weights at the 95th percentile, gives the weighted difference in means, fits a first causal forest, estimates propensity scores and splits the data into low / middle / high propensity segments (cut-offs 0.1 and 0.9; the middle segment has 575,120 people, 87%; the forests are seeded, so the segment is reproducible). Saves `capped_weights_segregated_workforce.Rdata` (input to Supp 3, 4 and 5), `numeric_age_truncated_data.Rdata` (input to Supp 5) and `X_age_truncated_data.Rdata` (saved, not currently loaded by any file) |
| `Supplementary_3_Analysis.Rmd` | Main causal analysis on the middle segment: pooled forest (out-of-bag predictions), separate forests for men and women, IPW and AIPW estimates (all / control / overlap targets), calibration, and heterogeneity of the gap by age, marital status, children, industry and education. Compares the estimators in one table |
| `Supplementary_4_segregated_workforce.Rmd` | The three propensity segments (mostly women / mixed / mostly men): who is in them, raw gaps (low 0.178, middle 0.189, high 0.099), occupation and industry segregation, and the gap by children in each segment |
| `Supplementary_5_Oaxaca-Blinder_Decomposition.Rmd` | Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition of the gap (twofold with a pooled reference, threefold, detailed by block) in five nested models, with bootstrap standard errors and weights; compared with the AIPW estimates and repeated within the propensity segments. The unexplained part with all covariates is 0.143 of a raw gap of 0.177 (19% explained) |
| `Supplementary_10_Some_background_on_Causal_Analysis.Rmd` | Background (no computations): potential outcomes, difference in means, direct, IPW and AIPW estimators, balance, calibration, overlap and the target populations used in Supp 2 to 5 |
| `cleanup.Rmd` | Shell commands, to paste one block at a time, to remove editor backups, LaTeX files and the intermediate data, to archive the project, and the sequence of `Rscript` commands that regenerates the analysis |
| `report.Rmd` | Full report. The numbers, tables and analysis figures are read from the `*_results.Rdata` files and `Supplementary_N_figs/` (run Supp 2-5 and `weights.Rmd` first) |
| `report_brief.Rmd` | Shorter version of the report (figures from `Supplementary_3_figs/`, `Supplementary_4_figs/`; segment shares read from the Supp 4 results) |
| `gender_wage_gap_report_brief.Rmd` | Older copy of `report_brief.Rmd` from before the October 2026 edits (old numbers, figures from `~/script8.6`); superseded, can be deleted |
| `report_beamer.Rmd` | Beamer slide deck: "Machine Learning and Causal Inference for Policy Evaluation" (estimates read from the Supp 2/3 results; the two counterfactual-density slides are switched off because their figures, from an old `script2/`, are not in the project) |
| `weights.Rmd` | Do the Census weights matter? Distribution of the weights (design effect 1.64 raw, 1.41 capped), weighted vs unweighted difference in means, regression and IPW estimates (5–8% lower with weights), and a weight-by-covariate interaction test. Reads `processing_files/X_ordered_numeric_...Rdata`, writes `weights_results.Rdata` and `weights_tests.txt` |
| `handling_categorical_variables.Rmd` | Why the categorical variables are coded as levels ordered by mean log wage. A runnable simulation (after a Win-Vector example that is not part of the project) and a comparison on the wage data of `ranger`'s default, `"order"`, one-hot and `vtreat`; notes on target-encoding leakage and on the sufficient-representations paper (not run). Not part of the argument of Supp 1–5. The first version (December 2024) is in the git history |

# How to run the Supplementary files

Supplementary 2 to 5 and `weights.Rmd` and `handling_categorical_variables.Rmd` share one structure.

- **Flags** in the setup chunk. `eval_flag` is TRUE to run the analysis (needs `processing_files/` and, for Supp 2 to 5, a lot of memory) and FALSE to knit the text and tables from the saved results file. `fig_eval_flag` (forced FALSE when `eval_flag` is FALSE) runs the chunks that write the figures. The input files, output files, flags and figures of each file are listed in the comment block at its top.
- **Unit tests.** Chunks named `tests_*` call `run_test("description", {...})` (`testthat`); a failing test means a statement in the text or an assumption of the analysis no longer holds. The last chunk of each file writes `<file>_tests.txt` and `<file>_session.txt`.
- **Saved results.** Every number in the text and tables is kept in a list `res`, saved to `Supplementary_N_results.Rdata` (and `weights_results.Rdata`, `handling_categorical_variables_results.Rdata`). Knitting with `eval_flag <- FALSE` loads it, so a PDF can be made without the data. The figures are PNG files in `Supplementary_N_figs/`.
- **Order.** Supp 1 (once, from the raw data; `Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("Supplementary_1_...Rmd")'`) then Supp 2 (writes the segment and age-truncated files), then Supp 3, 4 and 5 in any order. Supp 5 optionally reads `Supplementary_2_results.Rdata` and `Supplementary_3_results.Rdata` for comparisons. `weights.Rmd` and `handling_categorical_variables.Rmd` need only the Supp 1 output.
- **HPC.** `salloc --account=<ACCOUNT> --mem=120GB --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=32 -J interactive -t 4:00:00 srun --cpus-per-task=32 --pty /bin/bash -l`, then `module load pandoc texlive` (memory: 120 GB covers the 74 GB peak seen; Supp 1 needs about 20 GB; use partition `h24`, not `h2`). Run the files from the project directory, since all paths are relative to it.
- **Test results.** All tests pass in the HPC run of 20 October 2026: Supp 2 (24), Supp 3 (55), Supp 4 (22), Supp 5 (12), `weights.Rmd` (7) and `handling_categorical_variables.Rmd` (6). All of Supp 2 to 5 use the same seeded segmentation (middle segment 575,120).

# Files saved by `Supplementary_1_The_PUBS_data_and_preprocessing.Rmd`


All are written to `processing_files/` (the variable `wage_file_outputs`). Where each is used was checked by reading the `.Rmd` files, not by inspecting the files on disk.

There are two analysis data sets:

- `Xtrain_500000_20.Rdata`: a random sample of 500,000 rows in which 8 of the 13 covariates are factors (occupation reduced to 23 levels, industry to 20).
- `X_ordered_numeric_1061763_industry_269.Rdata`: the full data set (1,061,763 rows) with 13 numeric covariates, keeping the full 529 occupation and 269 industry levels.

**How factors are turned into numeric variables.** Many of the methods used (in particular GRF) need numeric covariates, and one-hot encoding 529 occupations is impractical. Instead each factor is given a single numeric code that emulates `ranger`'s `respect.unordered.factors = "order"`:

1. For each of `race`, `citizenship`, `marital`, `economic_region`, `occupation` and `industry`, compute the mean log hourly wage of each level over the full cleaned data set.
2. Sort the levels by that mean and recode them $1, \dots, k$, so level 1 has the lowest mean wage and level $k$ the highest.
3. `hispanic_origin` and `nativity` are binary and are recoded 0/1. `education_level` was already converted to approximately years of schooling in Supp 1.

The ordering is done once on the full data set, before any split. (An earlier version ordered train and test separately, which gave different codes in each.) Two consequences: the codes are only meaningful as a wage ranking, not as distances, and they are computed from the outcome, so they are a form of target encoding using the unweighted mean. `handling_categorical_variables.Rmd` measures the resulting leakage on 30,000-row subsamples (about 2% of the test error, within sampling error) and expects it to be smaller with a million rows; Supp 5 merges levels with fewer than 30 people of either gender. The codes are therefore not comparable with the original PUMS codes, and the mapping back to descriptions is saved in `variable_mappings.Rdata` (see below). The alternatives (`ranger`'s default, `"order"` and `"partition"`, one-hot, `vtreat`) are compared in `handling_categorical_variables.Rmd` (compiled to `handling_categorical_variables.pdf`); the method used here corresponds to its "order" setting, which gave the lowest test error among the methods that need no cross-fitting.

In more detail:

| File | Objects | Contents | Used in |
|------|---------|----------|---------|
| `Xtrain_500000_20.Rdata` | `Xtrain`, `W`, `Y`, `weights_supplied`, `weights_dummy` | Random sample of 500,000 rows (seed 124), excluding region "Abroad". `Xtrain` has 13 covariates: 8 factors (occupation reduced to 23 levels, industry to 20) and 5 numeric. `Y` is log hourly wage, `W` is 1 for male, `weights_supplied` are the Census weights, `weights_dummy` is all 1s. | Loaded by Supp 2 only, to save an age-truncated copy (`X_age_truncated_data.Rdata`); that copy is not loaded by any file at present. Not used by Supp 3 to 5, `weights.Rmd`, or the reports. |
| `X_ordered_numeric_1061763_industry_269.Rdata` | `Y`, `W`, `X_ordered_numeric`, `weights_supplied`, `weights_dummy` | Full cleaned sample of 1,061,763 rows, 13 numeric covariates. `race`, `citizenship`, `marital`, `economic_region`, `occupation` (529 levels) and `industry` (269 levels) are recoded 1 to $k$ in increasing order of mean log wage; `hispanic_origin` and `nativity` are 0/1. | Loaded by Supp 2, which is the source of everything Supp 3, 4 and 5 use (`numeric_age_truncated_data.Rdata`, `capped_weights_segregated_workforce.Rdata`). Also loaded by `weights.Rmd` and `handling_categorical_variables.Rmd`. |
| `industry_mapping_full_description.Rdata` | `industry_mapping_full_description` | Data frame (`original_code`, `new_code`, `description`) mapping the 1 to 269 industry codes back to NAICS codes and names. | Loaded by Supp 3 and Supp 4 (industry labels). Also inside `variable_mappings.Rdata`. |
| `occupation_mapping_full_description.Rdata` | `occupation_mapping_full_description` | The same mapping for the 529 occupation codes (SOC). | Loaded by Supp 4 (occupation labels). |
| `variable_mappings.Rdata` | `race_mapping`, `citizenship_mapping`, `marital_mapping`, `economic_region_mapping`, `industry_mapping_full_description`, `occupation_mapping_full_description` | All six code-to-description mappings together. | Loaded by Supp 4 (`race_mapping` only is used there). The citizenship, marital and economic-region mappings are not referenced anywhere; Supp 3 and 4 hard-code the marital labels. |

Saves in Supp 1 that are commented out (not produced): `X_1061763_15_industry_271_temp.Rdata`, and the `Xtest*` files. None of the reports, `Supplementary_10`, `handling_categorical_variables.Rmd`, `report_beamer.Rmd` or `gender_wage_gap_report_brief.Rmd` load any Supp 1 output. Supp 1 runs as a script (the old and exploratory chunks keep `eval=FALSE`); its mapping chunk saves the occupation descriptions as character rather than list columns (Supp 4 still converts them defensively with `as_character_column()`) and its tests, including those of the mappings, are in `Supplementary_1_tests.txt`. The `citizenship` mapping test used to fail because `citizenship` is numeric in `X`; the test now takes the levels from the values.
